newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Caution keeps Taiwan's China investment small.
newsitem.headline: Caution keeps Taiwan's China investment small.

text.p: Taiwan approved nine new investment projects for China on Friday, but said the small size of the deals reflected the government's caution over economic ties with its political rival.
The Economics Ministry said in a statement that it reviewed 11 applications in a meeting on Friday and approved nine of them worth a combined US$19.49 million.

Of the nine projects, three were by Tong Yang Industry Co Ltd, which planned to invest US$5 million, US$2.5 million and US$6.5 million respectively in three different plastic projects in China, the ministry said.
Also approved was Eternal Chemical Co Ltd's US$3 million investment in a synthetic resin project in China, the ministry said. The remaining investments were by smaller firms.
The number and scale of approved investments so far in April appear to have shrunk from March, when 15 projects worth a total of US$149.6 million were authorised, investment officials said.

"Large companies have slowed down their investment pace in mainland China because of the government's cautious policy," Tsai Lien-sheng, executive secretary of the Investment Commission, said on state television.
Criteria drafted by scholars and economists to regulate Taiwan's investment on the mainland will be discussed between the government and large companies, economics officials said.
Taiwan, which has banned direct contact with China since the end of the civil war that split them in 1949, has been concerned that its economy may become overdependent on China.
Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui on Thursday told a group of Japanese journalists that the government would remain cautious on investment policies toward China.
"Any investment in the mainland must be careful," Lee was quoted as saying in a statement released by the Presidential Office.
Some 30,000 Taiwanese firms have poured US$30 billion of investment into China since an unofficial thaw in bilateral relations began in the late 1980s.
But Taipei is concerned that too much dependence on China's massive market could make the island politically vulnerable to its arch rival.

Taiwan, which allows indirect investment in China, has said it would not further relax investment restrictions in China unless political tensions eased and China stopped disrupting the island's bid to increase its international profile.
China, which views Taiwan as a rebel-held province, has pressed other countries not to forge ties with Taiwan or permit visits by senior Taipei officials.
